catalog_quote: [Dettweiler 2015:34-35] C'Lela has two levels of lexical tone, namely high [H] and low [L]. This is illustrated in (223) for monosyllabic noun roots and in (224) for disyllabic noun roots. Note the minimal pairs in (223e & k) showing emic contrast between [gé] 'river' and [gè] 'species of tree', with H and L tone patterns respectively. ... Another feature of C'Lela is the occurrence, primarily in disyllabic noun roots, of a falling [HL] tone. The distribution of the HL tone appears to be restricted as follows: 1. It is almost always in a word-final CV syllable where the V is phonetically long (vowel length was confirmed with speech analyzer software). 2. The preceding (penultimate) syllable is always low tone. 3. The penultimate syllable is almost always either a CVC syllable, or a CV syllable with a long vowel in the nucleus ... [Aliero 2013:19-20] C'lela, like many other African languages, is a tone language. There are two basic contrastive tones; high tone and low tone, with a third one perceived as falling tone. ... Tones in C'lela are associated with a tone bearing unit, which is realized on syllables and the tone marks are assigned on vowels of such syllables. Tone performs both lexical and grammatical functions in the language. [Aliero 2013:179] C'lela, unlike English, does not use stress in distinguishing a compound from a phrase;
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

(1) Dettweiler 2015, SIL, 155 pp.): extracted text of p.38 = printed p.34 gives sec. 2.8 'Lexical Tone' opening exactly as quoted: "C'Lela has two levels of lexical tone, namely high [H] and low [L]. This is illustrated in (223) for monosyllabic noun roots and in (224) for disyllabic noun roots." and on p.35 "Another feature of C'Lela is the occurrence, primarily in disyllabic noun roots, of a falling [HL] tone." with the three distributional restrictions (word-final CV with phonetically long V; preceding syllable always L; penult almost always CVC or CV:). I read the whole of ch.2 (secs 2.1-2.10: phonemes, syllable/word patterns, ambiguous…
new_statements.rule_in_words: All accessible first-hand descriptions analyse C'lela as a register-tone language (H, L, plus a restricted falling HL on long final syllables after a low penult; grammatical tone in verb inflection). None of them states where word stress falls or whether a word accent exists; the only use of the word 'stress' is Aliero's comparative remark that C'lela does not use (compound) stress to distinguish compounds from phrases. No positive or negative word-stress rule can be extracted.
new_statements.exceptions: none (no stress rule given). Tone-related distributional facts only: falling HL almost always on a word-final CV syllable with phonetically long vowel, preceded by a low, usually heavy (CVC or CVV) penult (Dettweiler 2015:35-36); heavy syllable types concentrate in root-initial syllables (2015:18-19).
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern lexical tone on noun/verb roots in citation form (Zuru dialect) and grammatical tone in verbal morphology; falling tone described as phrase-final in Dettweiler 2012 App. A.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the Zuru dialect of C'lela (the reference dialect chosen for writing; Dettweiler 2000 fn., Dettweiler 2015 sec.1.3), i.e. the language-level languoid clel1238 [dri]; older literature calls it Dakarkari/Dakarci/Lela.
